title: Sliced Optimal Transport on the Sphere

blocks.heading: Abstract
blocks.text: Sliced optimal transport reduces optimal transport on multi-dimensional domains to transport on the line. More precisely, sliced optimal transport is the concatenation of the well-known Radon transform and the cumulative density transform, which analytically yields the solutions of the reduced transport problems. Inspired by this concept, we propose two adaptions for optimal transport on the 2-sphere. Firstly, as counterpart to the Radon transform, we introduce the vertical slice transform, which integrates along all circles orthogonal to a given direction. Secondly, we introduce a semicircle transform, which integrates along all half great circles with an appropriate weight function. Both transforms are generalized to arbitrary measures on the sphere. While the vertical slice transform can be combined with optimal transport on the interval and leads to a sliced Wasserstein distance restricted to even probability measures, the semicircle transform is related to optimal transport on the circle and results in a different sliced Wasserstein distance for arbitrary probability measures. The applicability of both novel sliced optimal transport concepts on the sphere is demonstrated by proof-of-concept examples dealing with the interpolation and classification of spherical probability measures. The numerical implementation relies on the singular value decompositions of both transforms and fast Fourier techniques. For the inversion with respect to probability measures, we propose the minimization of an entropy-regularized Kullback--Leibler divergence, which can be numerically realized using a primal-dual proximal splitting algorithm.

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.text: Optimal transport and in particular Wasserstein distances between measures have received much attention from a theoretical and practical point of view [PeyCut19, San15, Vil03] and recently became of interest in neural gradient flows [FZTC2022, KSB2022, AHS2023]. While Wasserstein distances are in general hard to compute, there exist analytic formulas for optimal transport on the line. Therefore sliced Wasserstein distances, which basically combine the Radon transform in Euclidean spaces with optimal transport on the line, have become quite popular [RabPeyDelBer12, San15, NRNRNH23]. In particular, the related Radon cumulative distribution transform has been applied for interpolation and classification as well as for model reduction [KolParRoh16, GuaLiaDuYin19, RenWolMao21, ShiRub21, BRPP15]. The idea behind sliced optimal transport has been generalized and transferred to many related problems. There exists sliced variants [BC19, BSTK23] of partial optimal transport [Fig10, CAG20], where only a fraction of mass is transported, and a sliced version [CTP+21] of multi-marginal optimal transport [GS98, BLNS22, BBS22], considering the transport between several measures instead of only two. For optimal transport on Riemannian manifolds, sliced Wasserstein distances based on the push-forward of the eigenfunctions of the Laplacian have been proposed in [RusMaj20]. Especially for shape and graph analysis, sliced optimal transport has been transferred to the Gromov Wasserstein setting [VFC+19], which more generally defines a metric between metric measure spaces [Mem11, Stu20, BeBeSt22]. Differently from the Wasserstein formulation with its analytic solution, the Gromov Wasserstein transport on the line is more involved [BCS22, DLV23]

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.text: In this paper, we transfer the slicing approach to optimal transport on the two-dimensional sphere. Spherical optimal transport has been intensely studied in recent years. For instance, the problem can be solved using a Monge Ampère type equation [HamTur22, McrCotBud18, WelBroBudCul16] or a variational framework [CuiQi19]. The regularity of optimal maps has been investigated in [Loe10]. Spherical Wasserstein barycenters have been computed using a stochastic projected subgradient method [StaClaSolJeg17] and have been estimated on random graphs [TheKer22]

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.text: To introduce slicing frameworks on the sphere, we do not follow the Laplacian approach in [RusMaj20], but focus on spherical counterparts of the Radon transform. A well-known one is the Funk Radon transform [Fun13, Hel11, LoRiSpSp11, QueWeiHubErc23], which takes integrals along all great circles. Integration along all circles of a fixed radius were studied in [Sch69, Rub00]. Further Radon-type transforms were considered based on intersections with planes containing a fixed point inside the sphere [Pal16, Sal17, Qu17, Que20], on the sphere [AbDa93, Rub22], and outside the sphere [AgRu20]. Moreover, transforms including derivatives were proposed in [MaMaOd01, QuHiLo18]. However, in the context of sliced optimal transport, we require that probability density functions on the sphere are mapped to a family of probability density functions on one-dimensional domains. For this purpose, we consider two specific spherical transforms, namely the vertical slice transform and the normalized semicircle transform

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.text: The vertical slice transform was first considered in [GiReSh94] and applied in [ZaSc10, HiQu15circav] for photoacoustic tomography. The generalization to higher dimensions is due to [Rub19]. The basic idea is to take means along parallel circles, see fig: vertical_slice_1, which gives a probability density function on an interval. The process is then repeated for further directions. Geometrically, the areas of integration for a fixed direction can be imagined like an egg cutter applied to the sphere. We generalize the vertical slice transform to probability measures and use it to define a vertical sliced Wasserstein distance. Radon transforms of measures have been considered in the context of a dual fibration, cf. [GelShm83, Pal95] and [Chap. 2, § 2, Hel11], where they are defined via duality. We will see that our definition via the push-forward of measures can be also derived from that point of view

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.text: An (unnormalized) semicircle transform was examined in [Gro98, HiPoQu18]. It takes integrals along semicircles starting in a fixed point, see fig: vertical_slice_2, and yields a function defined on the one-dimensional unit circle. The process is then repeated for further starting points. This transform has been combined with optimal transport on the circle to obtain a sliced Wasserstein distance [Bon22]. However, the crucial point is here that the unnormalized semicircle transform does not map probability density functions to probability density functions, meaning that optimal transport techniques on the circle cannot be applied. In the numeric part of [Bon22], the authors restrict themselves to point measures, which then are projected onto great circles. This approach corresponds to an appropriately normalized semicircle transform instead, where the integrand is multiplied with a certain weight function. In this paper, we introduce and study this normalized semicircle transform in a rigours manner to obtain a semicircular sliced Wasserstein distance

blocks.heading: Main contributions
blocks.text: start-of-itemize:. We give rigorous definitions of the vertical slice and the normalized semicircle transform, which are originally considered only for functions, and generalize them to measures using an appropriate push-forward. For absolutely continuous measures, the generalized and initial definitions coincide in the sense that merely the density function has to be transformed. Furthermore, probability measures are transformed to probability measures.. We prove a singular value decomposition of the normalized semicircle transform, which provides an approach for numerical computations. Moreover, the singular value decompositions of the vertical slice and the normalized semicircle transform allow the inversion via their Moore Penrose pseudoinverses.. We define sliced Wasserstein distances on the sphere based on both transform. We show that the normalized semicircle transform is injective for all measures, and hence the sliced Wasserstein distance indeed fulfills the properties of a metric. Furthermore, the vertical sliced Wasserstein distance is a metric for even measures on the sphere.. We propose a Tikhonov-type regularization which minimizes a variational model consisting of the entropy-regularized Kullback Leibler divergence. This ensures that the inverse is a probability measure and in particular non-negative. Further, this allows to compute a sliced CDT interpolation between spherical probability measures to approximate Wasserstein barycenters. end-of-itemize

blocks.heading: Outline of the Paper
blocks.text: We start in sec: prelim with the necessary preliminaries on optimal transport, the unit sphere and the rotation group on R^3. Then, we introduce the two counterparts of the Radon transform on S^2, namely the vertical slice transform in sec: vert_slice and the normalized semicircle transform in sec: semicircle. First, we define the transforms for functions and derive their adjoint operators and singular value decompositions on L^2(S^2). In order to combine these transforms with optimal transport on the interval and the circle respectively, we have to enlarge their definitions to measure spaces which we have not found in a mathematically rigorous form in the literature. sec: SOT connects the above transforms with optimal transport to introduce spherical sliced Wasserstein distances for measures on the sphere. sec: disc-and-inv deals with the discretization of the spherical transforms and their inversion, which is an ill-posed problem. For an approximate inversion, we can use the truncated Moore Penrose pseudoinverse. However, when dealing with probability density functions, this inversion does not guarantee the non-negativity of the reconstructed function. Therefore, we suggest another reconstruction which minimizes a variational model consisting of an entropy-regularized Kullback Leibler divergence, see sec: reg. The actual minimization can be done by a primal-dual splitting. Numerical proof-of-concept results are reported in sec: numerics, where we provide two kinds of experiments. First, we show in sec: int-meas that Wasserstein barycenters on the sphere can be approximated using sliced Wasserstein transforms and Wasserstein interpolation on the interval and the circle respectively. These results require in particular the inversion of the sliced spherical transforms. Second, we demonstrate by a synthetic example that the binary classification of different measures is in principle possible in sec: classification

blocks.heading: Preliminaries
blocks.text: In this section, we first provide the notation and necessary preliminaries on optimal transport, in particular on the interval and the circle. Then, we recall basic facts about the unit sphere and the rotation group on mathbb R^3

blocks.heading: Measures and Optimal Transport
blocks.text: Let X be a compact metric space with metric dcolon X times X to R, and let B(X) be the Borel sigma -algebra induced by d. By M(X), we denote the Banach space of signed, finite measures, and by P(X) the subset of probability measures on X. The pre-dual space of M(X) is C(X). Let Y be another compact metric space and Tcolon X to Y be measurable. For mu in M(X), we define the push-forward measure T_# mu coloneqq mu circ T^(-1) in M(mathbb Y). For any measure pi in M(X times Y) with first marginal mu in M(X), i. e., pi(B times Y) = mu(B) for all B in B(X), we call a collection of measures pi_x in M(Y), x in X, a disintegration family if int_(X times Y) f(x, y) d pi(x, y) = int_X int_Y f(x, y) d pi_x(y) d mu(x) for all measurable functions f on X times Y

blocks.heading: Measures and Optimal Transport
blocks.text: The p - Wasserstein distance, pin[1, infty), of mu, nu in P(mathbb X) is given by WS_p^p(mu, nu) coloneqq min_(piinPi(mu, nu)) int_(mathbb X^2) d^p(x, y) d pi (x, y), with Pi(mu, nu) coloneqq (pi inM(mathbb X times mathbb X): pi(B times mathbb X) = mu(B), pi(mathbb Xtimes B) = nu(B) for all B in B(mathbb X)). It defines a metric on P(mathbb X). The metric space P^p(mathbb X) coloneqq ( P(mathbb X), W_p) is called p -Wasserstein space and, in case p=2, just Wasserstein space. The above Wasserstein distance is just a special case of the more general optimal transport problem, where d^p(x, y) can be replaced by a more general cost function c(x, y). For deltain[0,1], the p -Wasserstein barycenter between mu, nuinP^p(X) is the minimizer of min_(omegainP(X)) (1-delta) WS_p^p(mu, omega) + delta WS_p^p(nu, omega), see [AguCar11]. Note that the Wasserstein barycenter between absolutely continuous measures is unique, cf. [KimPas17]

blocks.heading: Optimal Transport on the Interval
blocks.text: If X is the unit interval II coloneqq [-1,1] with the distance d(x, y) = x-y, the optimal transport between two probability measures mu, nuin P(II) can be computed easily [PeyCut19, San15, Vil03] using the cumulative distribution function F_mu(x) coloneqq mu([-1,x]), xinII, which is non-decreasing and right-continuous. Its pseudoinverse, the quantile function F_mu^(-1)(r) coloneqq min( xinII: F_mu(x)ge r), rin[0,1], is non-decreasing and left-continuous. The measure mu can be recovered by mu = (F_mu^(-1))_# sigma_([0,1]), where sigma_([0,1]) denotes the Lebesque measure on [0,1]. The p -Wasserstein distance between mu, nu in P^p(II) now equals WS_p(mu, nu) = lVert F_mu^(-1) - F_nu^(-1) rVert_(L^p([0,1])). Moreover, if mu in Pac(II), where Pac(II) denotes the probability measures that are absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure, then the optimal transport plan pi in is uniquely given by pi = (Id, T^(mu, nu))_# mu quadtext(with)quad T^(mu, nu)(x) coloneqq F_nu^(-1)(F_mu(x)), quad x in II

blocks.heading: Optimal Transport on the Interval
blocks.text: Based on the optimal transport map T^(mu, nu), the Wasserstein space P^p(II) can be isometrically embedded into L^p_omega(II) with omega in Pac(II) [KolParRoh16, PaKoSo18, BeBeSt22], where L^p_omega(II) consists of all p -integrable functions with respect to omega. More precisely, for the reference measure omega in Pac(II), the cumulative distribution transform (CDT) is defined by CDT_omega colon P^p(II) to L^p_omega(II) with CDT_(omega)[mu] (x) coloneqq (T^(omega, mu) - Id)(x) = bigl(F_(mu)^(-1) circ F_(omega) bigr) (x) - x, quad xinII, and we especially have WS_p(mu, nu) = lVert CDT_omega[mu] - CDT_(omega)[nu] rVert_(L^p_omega(II)). The CDT is in fact a mapping from P^p(II) into the tangent space of P^p(II) at omega, see [§ 8.5, AGS05]. Due to the relation to the optimal transport map, the CDT can be inverted by mu = CDT^(-1)_omega[h] coloneqq (h + Id)_# omega for h = CDT_omega[mu]. If mu, omega in Pac(II) possess the density functions f_mu > 0, f_omega > 0, then, by the transformation formula for push-forward measures, f_mu can be recovered by f_mu(x) = left( g^(-1) right)'(x) f_omega(g^(-1)(x)) quad text(with) quad g(x) = CDT_omega[mu](x) + x, quad x in II. For mu, nu in P(II), and an arbitrary reference measure omega in Pac(II), the 2-Wasserstein barycenter has the form CDT^(-1)_(omega)left( delta CDT_omega [nu] + (1-delta) CDT_omega[mu] right), see [KolParRoh16]. In particular for omega = mu, we have by that CDT_mu[mu](x) = F_mu^(-1)(F_mu(x))-x = 0 and therefore the barycenter becomes CDT^(-1)_(mu)left( delta CDT_mu [nu] right)

blocks.heading: Optimal Transport on the Circle
blocks.text: On the circle T coloneqq R/(2piZ) equipped with the metric d(x, y) coloneqq min_(kinZ) x-y+2pi k, the optimal transport can be computed in a similar manner by incorporating the periodicity. Following [DelSalSob10, RabDelGou11], we define the (extended) cumulative distribution function by tilde F_mu(x) coloneqq mu([0,x]) for x in [0,2pi] and extend it to mathbb R by the convention tilde F_mu(x + 2pi) coloneqq tilde F_mu(x) + 1. Its pseudoinverse, the (extended) quantile function, is defined as tilde F_mu^(-1)(r) coloneqq min( xinR: tilde F_mu(x)ge r) for rin R. Note that tilde F and tilde F^(-1) are mappings defined on entire R. The p -Wasserstein distance between mu, nu in P(T) is given by W_p^p(mu, nu) = min_(thetainR) int_(0)^(1) lverttilde F_mu^(-1)(r) - (tilde F_nu - theta)^(-1)(r) rvert^p d r, where (tilde F_nu - theta)^(-1) is the pseudoinverse of the shifted cumulative distribution function [RabDelGou11]. For mu in Pac(T), each minimizer theta of yields an optimal transport plan pi = (Id, iota(tilde T^(mu, nu)))_# mu quadtext(with)quad tilde T^(mu, nu)(x) coloneqq (tilde F_nu - theta)^(-1) (tilde F_mu(x)), quad x in [0, 2pi), where iota colon R to T denotes the canonical projection from the line to the circle. Note that tilde T^(mu, nu)(x) in R is the representative of iota(tilde T^(mu, nu)(x)) in T with d(x, iota(tilde T^(mu, nu)(x))) = lvert x - tilde T^(mu, nu)(x) rvert. If p>1 and mu, nuinPac(T), the minimizer theta of is unique. This follows by the proof of [Lem. 5.2, DelSalSob10], where it is shown that the objective of is convex in theta, but the argument even implies strict convexity. In analogy to, we define for pin(1, infty), the circular CDT (cCDT) of muinPac(T) with reference measure omegainPac(T) by sCDT_omega colon P^p(T) to L^p_omega(T) with sCDT_(omega)[mu] (x) coloneqq (tilde T^(omega, mu) - Id)(x) = bigl((tilde F_(mu)-theta_(omega, mu))^(-1) circ tilde F_(omega)bigr) (x) - x, quad xin[0, 2pi), where tilde T^(omega, mu) is the optimal transport plan and theta_(omega, mu) the minimizer of. Note that the cCDT is no longer an isometric embedding. The cCDT can be inverted by mu = sCDT^(-1)_omega[h] coloneqq (iota circ(h + Id))_#omega for h = sCDT_omega[mu]. If mu, omega in Pac(T) have densities f_mu > 0, f_omega > 0, the density f_mu can be recovered similarly to via f_mu(x) = left( g^(-1)right)'(x) f_omega(g^(-1)(x)) quad text(with) quad g(x) = iota left(sCDT_omega[mu](x) + x right), quad x in T. In analogy to with omega = mu, we interpolate between the measures mu, nu in Pac(T) by sCDT^(-1)_(mu)[delta sCDT_(mu)[nu]]

blocks.heading: Unit  Sphere
blocks.text: The two-dimensional unit sphere is defined as S^(2) coloneqq (bx inR^3: bx =1). The canonical unit vectors are henceforth denoted by zb e^j, j=1, 2, 3. Points bxi in S^2 can be parameterized in spherical coordinates bxi = sph(varphi, vartheta) coloneqq left( cosvarphi sinvartheta, sinvarphi sinvartheta, cosvarthetaright) in S^2, quad varphiinT, varthetain[0,pi]. The restriction sphcolon left(Ttimes (0, pi) right) cup left((0)times(0, pi ) right) to mathbb S^2 is a bijective mapping. We denote the first and second component of this restriction as azimuth angle azi(bxi) and zenith angle zen(bxi), respectively, which are uniquely given by azi(sph(varphi, vartheta)) = varphi quadtext(and)quad zen(sph(varphi, vartheta)) = vartheta for all (varphi, vartheta) in left(Ttimes (0, pi) right) cup left((0)times(0, pi ) right). The surface measure sigma_(S^2) on the sphere is given by int_(S^2) f(bxi) dsigma_(S^2)(bxi) = int_(0)^(pi) int_(T) f(sph(varphi, vartheta)) sinvartheta dvarphi d vartheta. Normalizing sigma_(S^2) yields the uniform measure u_(S^2) coloneqq (4pi)^(-1) sigma_(S^2). We denote by L^(p)(S^2), p in [1,infty], the Banach space of all (equivalence classes of) p -integrable functions on S^2, where we use the above surface measure

The spherical harmonics (Y_n^k: ninNN, k= -n,, dots, n) form an orthonormal basis of L^2(mathbb S^2). blocks.heading: Vertical Slice Transform of Functions
blocks.text: In analogy to the Radon transform, the main idea behind the vertical slice transform is to integrate a given function f colon S^2 to R along parallel vertical slices. To describe these slices mathematically, we define the slicing operator cS_psi colon S^2 to II for any fixed psi in T by cS_psi (zb xi) coloneqq langle bxi, (cos psi, sin psi, 0)^tT rangle = cos(psi) xi_1 + sin(psi) xi_2, and the corresponding slice / circle by C_(psi)^(t) coloneqq cS_psi^(-1)(t) = (zb xi in mathbb S^2: cS_psi (zb xi) = t), quad t in II. The slice C_(psi)^(t) is the intersection of mathbb S^2 and the plane with normal (cos psi, sin psi, 0)^tT and distance t from the origin, An illustration of the slices C_psi^t for fixed psi is given in fig: vertical_slice_1. The vertical slice transform V is defined by mathcal V f(psi, t) coloneqq frac(1)(2 pi sqrt(1-t^2)) int_(C_(psi)^(t)) f(zbxi) ds (bxi), qquad psiinT, tin (-1, 1), where d s denotes the arc-length on C_(psi)^(t). For t = pm 1, the vertical slice transform is mathcal V f (psi, 1) coloneqq f(cospsi, sinpsi, 0) quadtext(and)quad mathcal V f (psi, -1) coloneqq f(-cospsi, -sinpsi, 0). For fixed psi in T, we define the (normalized) restrictions V_psicoloneqq 2pi V(psi, cdot). This corresponds to projecting the mean values of f along C_(psi)^(t) to t in II. For an illustration see again fig: vertical_slice_1. The different normalizations of V and V_psi are chosen with respect to the later generalization to measures and ensure that density functions are transformed to density functions by V and V_psi. By the following proposition, both operators are well defined almost everywhere

blocks.heading: Vertical Slice Transform of Functions
blocks.text: Since all circles C_(psi)^(t) are symmetric with respect to the xi_1 - xi_2 plane, V f vanishes for functions f which are odd in the third coordinate, i. e., f(xi_1, xi_2, xi_3) = - f(xi_1, xi_2, -xi_3). For brevity, we call these functions odd. In [GiReSh94], an explicit inversion formula for even functions, i. e., f(xi_1, xi_2, xi_3) = f(xi_1, xi_2, -xi_3), is derived. However, as for the Radon inversion formula, this formula leads to instable practical computations if we leave the range of V. For numerical simulation, we will invert V using its singular value decomposition. For this purpose, notice that the spherical harmonics Y^k_n with even k+n are even functions, while those with odd k+n are odd functions

blocks.text: start-of-theorem: [ [Thm. 3.3, HiQu15circav] ] The vertical slice transform fulfills V Y_n^k (psi, t) = mathrm(v)_n^k sqrt(tfrac(2n+1)(4 pi)) e^(i k psi) P_n(t), qquad ninNN, kin(-n, dots, n), n+ktext( even), where mathrm(v)_n^k coloneqq (-1)^(frac(n+k)2) sqrt(frac((n-k)! )((n+k)! )) frac((n+k-1)!! ) ((n-k)!! ). There exist constants C_1, C_2>0 such that for all ninNN, kin(-n, dots, n) with n+k even, C_1(n+1/2)^(-1/2) le lvert mathrm(v)_n^krvert le C_2(n+1/2)^(-1/4). end-of-theorem

blocks.text: Noting that the functions B_n^k(psi, t) coloneqq sqrt(frac(2n+1)(4pi)) P_n(t) e^(i k psi), qquad forall (psi, t) in Ttimes II, form an orthonormal basis of L^2(T times II) and that v _n^k to 0 as n to infty, we deduce that Vcolon L^2(S^2) to L^2(T times II) is a compact operator with singular value decomposition V f (psi, t) = sum_(n in (mathbb N_0)) sum_(substack(k=-n +k text(even)) )^n mathrm(v)_n^k B_n^k(psi, t). blocks.text: For functions fcolon S^2toR, the vertical slice transform V f(psi, t) in and its restriction V_psi f(t) in are integrals of f along the slices cS_psi^(-1)(t). Heuristically, the related concept for measures mu in M(S^2) would be to consider mu(cS_psi^(-1)(t)). In this manner, for a fixed angle psi in T, we generalize the (restricted) vertical slice transform V_psi by V_psi colon M(S^2) to M(II), quad mu mapsto (cS_psi)_# mu = mu circ cS_psi^(-1). In the function setting, we figuratively obtain V f by gluing the (rescaled) functions 1 (2pi)V_psi f together along the angle psi. In the measure setting, the corresponding concept is to consider V_psi as disintegration family. We define the vertical slice transform Vcolon M(S^2) to M(T times II) by V mu coloneqq (T_(V))_# (u_(T) times mu) quadtext(with)quad T_(V)(psi, zbxi) coloneqq (psi, cS_psi(zbxi)). The disintegration aspect becomes clear in the following proposition

blocks.heading: Normalized Semicircle Transform of Functions
blocks.text: Instead of integrating over parallel slices, the semicircle transform integrates a function along all meridians with respect to a fixed zenith on the sphere. For any zenith sph(alpha, beta)inS^2 with alpha in T and beta in [0,pi], we define the azimuth operator cA_(alpha, beta)colon S^2 to T and the zenith operator cZ_(alpha, beta)colon S^2 to [0, pi] as cA_(alpha, beta)(bxi) &coloneqq azi(eul(alpha, beta, 0)^tT bxi), cZ_(alpha, beta)(bxi) &coloneqq zen(eul(alpha, beta, 0)^tT bxi), i. e., we rotate the zenith back to the north pole and take the azimuth and zenith angle, see fig: semicircles. For the zenith sph(alpha, beta) and fixed gamma in T, we consider the semicircles/meridians M_(alpha, beta)^gamma coloneqq cA_(alpha, beta)^(-1)(gamma) = (bxi in mathbb S^2: cA_(alpha, beta)(bxi) = gamma ). If gammaneq0, we have M_(alpha, beta)^gamma = ( bxi=eul(alpha, beta, 0) sph(gamma, vartheta) = eul(alpha, beta, gamma) sph(0, vartheta): vartheta in (0, pi) ). Otherwise, if gamma=0, we need to replace the open interval by a closed one, i. e., vartheta in [0,pi]. Figuratively, M_(alpha, beta)^gamma is a rotation of the meridian (sph(gamma, vartheta): vartheta in (0, pi)) with azimuth gamma by eul(alpha, beta, 0). The normalized semicircle transform W of f colon S^2 to R is defined by mathcal W f (alpha, beta, gamma) &coloneqq frac(1)(4pi) int_(M_(alpha, beta)^gamma) f(bxi) sinleft(cZ_(alpha, beta) ( bxi) right) ds(bxi) &= frac(1)(4pi) int_0^pi f(eul(alpha, beta, 0) sph(gamma, vartheta)) sin(vartheta) dx vartheta. We may interpret M_(alpha, beta)^gamma as rotation of the prime median by eul(alpha, beta, gamma). Based on the substitution bQ = eul(alpha, beta, gamma), the normalized semicircle transform defines a function on SO via mathcal W f (bQ) coloneqq frac(1)(4pi) int_(0)^(pi) fleft(bQ sph(0, vartheta) right) sin(vartheta) dx vartheta. Henceforth, we will not distinguish between W f(alpha, beta, gamma) and W f(bQ). Especially for the inversion formula by the singular value decomposition, we will make use of the latter definition. The multiplication with (4pi)^(-1) sin (vartheta) in the latitude ensures that density functions are mapped to density functions allowing the later generalization to measures. For the zenith sph(alpha, beta), we define the (normalized) restriction W_(alpha, beta) f coloneqq 4pi W f(alpha, beta, cdot)

blocks.heading: Normalized Semicircle Transform of Functions
blocks.text: start-of-remark: The (unnormalized) semicircle transform W colon C(S^2)to C(SO) is defined by widetilde (mathcal W) f(bQ) coloneqq int_(-pi/2)^(pi/2) fleft(smash(bQ^tT (sph(varphi, tfracpi2)))right) dvarphi, qquad bQinSO, see [HiPoQu18]. It computes the mean values of f along all half great circles of the sphere, i. e., without the weight sin(vartheta) of. The injectivity of W was shown in [Gro98]. A singular value decomposition and inversion algorithms were provided in [HiPoQu18]. The authors of [Bon22] reinvented this transform with another parameterization using the plane through Psi(alpha, beta, 0) zb e^1 and Psi(alpha, beta, 0) zb e^2. More precisely, their notation was not clear to us since it seems that they have applied the normalized transform in the numerical examples, but certain parts in their analysis rely on the unnormalized transform. end-of-remark

blocks.text: The semicircle transforms W and W_(alpha, beta) are well defined for continuous functions as well as for p -integrable functions. Moreover, both transforms are continuous operators

blocks.heading: Normalized Semicircle Transform of Functions
blocks.text: start-of-proposition: Let 1 le p le infty, and let sph(alpha, beta) in S^2. For every f in L^p(S^2), it holds int_(T) W_(alpha, beta) f(gamma) dx gamma = int_(S^2) f(zbxi) dxsigma_(S^2)(zbxi) quadtext(and)quad int_(SO) W f(bQ) dsigma_(SO)(bQ) = int_(S^2) f(zbxi) dxsigma_(S^2)(zbxi). The operators W_(alpha, beta) colon L^p(S^2) to L^p(T) and W colon L^p(S^2) to L^p(SO) are bounded with lVert W_(alpha, beta) rVert_(L^p to L^p) le 2^(1-1/p) quadtext(and)quad lVert W rVert_(L^p to L^p) le (2pi)^(1/p - 1). Moreover, it holds W_(alpha, beta) colon C(S^2) to C(T) and W colon C(S^2) to C(SO). end-of-proposition

blocks.heading: Normalized Semicircle Transform of Functions
blocks.text: start-of-proof: Since the surface measure on S^2 is invariant under rotations, we have int_(T) mathcal W_(alpha, beta) f(gamma) dxgamma &= int_(T) int_(0)^(pi) f ( eul(alpha, beta, 0) sph(gamma, vartheta) ) sin(vartheta) d vartheta dgamma &= int_(S^2) f ( eul(alpha, beta, 0) bxi ) dsigma_(S^2) (bxi) = int_(S^2) f (bxi) dsigma_(S^2)(bxi). The definition of W_(alpha, beta) and integration over alpha and beta gives the second identity. Thus W_(alpha, beta) and W are well defined almost everywhere by Fubini's theorem. Using absolute values and the triangle inequality in the above computation yields lVert W_(alpha, beta) rVert_(L^1 to L^1) = lVert W rVert_(L^1 to L^1) = 1, where we deduce a lower bound of the norm by inserting the constant f=1. The semicircle transform is further essentially bounded by lvert W_(alpha, beta) f(gamma) rvert le int_(0)^pi lvert fleft( eul(alpha, beta, 0) sph(gamma, vartheta ) right)rvert sin(vartheta) dxvartheta le 2 esssup_(bxi in S^2) lvert f(bxi) rvert; so lVert W_(alpha, beta) rVert_(L^infty to L^infty) = 2 and lVert W rVert_(L^infty to L^infty) = (2pi)^(-1). The second assertion now follows from the Riesz Thorin interpolation theorem. The last assertion is an immediate consequence of Lebesgue's dominated convergence theorem. end-of-proof

(n+j-1)!! )( (n-j)!! (n+1)!! ) 2: & n text( even), (pi): & n text( odd), lambda_n^(-j) coloneqq (-1)^j lambda_n^j, and lambda_n^j=0 otherwise. blocks.heading: Spherical Sliced Wasserstein Distances
blocks.text: The computation of the Wasserstein distance on the sphere consists in determining a transport plan between the considered probability measures. To avoid the occurring optimization problem, the general idea behind so-called sliced Wasserstein distances [KolNadSimBadRoh19, Bon22] is to transform the measures first to one-dimensional domains, and to exploit the explicit solution formula of the one-dimensional transport. Based on the vertical slice and the normalized semicircle transform, we can define two kinds of spherical sliced distances. For p in [1, infty) and mu, nu in M(S^2), we define the vertical sliced Wasserstein distance VSW_p^p(mu, nu) coloneqq int_(T) WS_p^p( V_(psi)mu, V_(psi)nu ) d psi, and the semicircular sliced Wasserstein distance SSW_p^p(mu, nu) coloneqq int_(S^2) WS_p^p( W_(alpha, beta)mu, W_(alpha, beta)nu ) d sigma_(S^2)(sph(alpha, beta)), which are integrals over Wasserstein distances on II and T, respectively

blocks.heading: Spherical Sliced Wasserstein Distances
blocks.text: start-of-theorem: For every 1 le p < infty, the vertical sliced Wasserstein distance VSW_p is a metric on M_(sym)(S^2), which was defined in, and the semicircular Wasserstein distance SSW_p is a metric on M(S^2). end-of-theorem

blocks.heading: Spherical Sliced Wasserstein Distances
blocks.text: start-of-proof: The symmetry and the triangle inequality follow from the corresponding properties of the Wasserstein distance and the p -norm on T and S^2. The positive definiteness follows from the injectivity of V and W in thm: V_inj and thm: B_inj. end-of-proof

blocks.heading: Spherical Sliced Wasserstein Distances
blocks.text: Since the geodesic distance d(zbxi, zbeta) = arccos(zbxi^topzbeta) on the sphere S^2 is rotationally invariant, i. e., d(zb Q zbxi, zb Q zbeta) = d(zbxi, zbeta) for all zb Q inSO, the Wasserstein distance on S^2 inherits this property, i. e., WS_p(mu, nu) = WS_p(mucirc zb Q, nucirc zb Q) for all zb QinSO. The vertical sliced Wasserstein distance is only partially rotation invariant

blocks.heading: Spherical Sliced Wasserstein Distances
blocks.text: start-of-proposition: For any pin[1, infty), the vertical sliced Wasserstein distance VSW_p is invariant with respect to rotations around the vertical axis, i. e., for all mu, nu in M(S^2) and alpha in T, it holds VSW_p(mu, nu) = VSW_p(mu circ zb R_3(alpha), mu circ zb R_3(alpha)). end-of-proposition

blocks.heading: Spherical Sliced Wasserstein Distances
blocks.text: start-of-proof: We have VSW_p^p(mu circ zb R_3(alpha), mu circ zb R_3(alpha)) &= int_(T) WS_p^p( V_(psi)[mu circ zb R_3(alpha)], V_(psi)[nucirc zb R_3(alpha)] ) d psi &= int_(T) WS_p^p( [cS_psi circ zb R_3(alpha)^tT]_#mu, [cS_psi circ zb R_3(alpha)^tT]_# nu ) d psi. Since [cS_psi circ zb R_3(alpha)^tT](bxi) = langle bxi, zb R_3(alpha) (cos psi, sin psi, 0)^tT rangle = cS_(psi + alpha)(bxi), we further obtain VSW_p^p(mu circ zb R_3(alpha), mu circ zb R_3(alpha)) = int_(T) WS_p^p( V_(psi + alpha) mu, V_(psi + alpha) nu ) d psi = VSW_p^p(mu, nu). qedhere end-of-proof

blocks.heading: Spherical Sliced Wasserstein Distances
blocks.text: In contrast to the vertical sliced Wasserstein distance, the semicircular sliced Wasserstein distance is invariant to general rotations

blocks.heading: Spherical Sliced Wasserstein Distances
blocks.text: start-of-proposition: For any pin[1, infty), the semicircular sliced Wasserstein distance SSW_p is rotationally invariant, i. e., for every mu, nu in M(S^2) and zb Q in SO, it holds SSW_p(mu, nu) = SSW_p(mu circ zb Q, mu circ zb Q). end-of-proposition

blocks.text: start-of-proof: For gamma in T, let cT_gamma colon T to T be the shift operator given by cT_gamma(psi) coloneqq psi - gamma. Exploiting the shift invariance of the Wasserstein distance on T, the identity, and the rotation invariance of the surface measure on SO, we have &SSW_p^p(mu circ zb Q, nu circ zb Q) = int_(S^2) WS_p^p( W_(alpha, beta)[mu circ zb Q], W_(alpha, beta)[nu circ zb Q] ) d sigma_(S^2)(sph(alpha, beta)) &quad= frac(1)(2pi) int_T int_(S^2) WS_p^p( [cT_gamma circ cA_(alpha,beta)]_# (mu circ zb Q), [cT_gamma circ cA_(alpha,beta)]_#(nu circ zb Q) ) d sigma_(S^2)(sph(alpha, beta)) d gamma &quad= frac(1)(2pi) int_(SO) WS_p^p( [azi(eul(alpha,beta,gamma)^tT zb Q^tT ]_# mu, [azi(eul(alpha,beta,gamma)^tT zb Q^tT cdot)]_# nu ) d sigma_(SO)(eul(alpha, beta, gamma)) &quad= frac(1)(2pi) int_(SO) WS_p^p( [azi(eul(tildealpha,tildebeta,tildegamma)^tT cdot)]_# mu, [azi(eul(tildealpha,tildebeta,tildegamma)^tT cdot)]_# nu ) d sigma_(SO)(eul(tildealpha, tildebeta, tildegamma)) &quad= frac(1)(2pi) int_T int_(S^2) WS_p^p( [cT_(tildegamma) circ cA_(tildealpha,tildebeta)]_# mu, [cT_(tildegamma) circ cA_(tildealpha,tildebeta)]_#nu) d sigma_(S^2)(sph(tildealpha, tildebeta)) d tildegamma = SSW_p^p(mu, nu). qedhere end-of-proof

blocks.heading: Discretization and Inversion via Moore Penrose Pseudoinverse
blocks.text: We will compute the sliced spherical transforms of (probability density) functions numerically based on the singular value decomposition in a similar way as in [HiPoQu18]. To this end, we need an appropriate discretization. In particular we need quadrature formulas on S^2 as well as on the image domains T times II and SO of V and W, respectively

blocks.heading: Discretization and Inversion via Moore Penrose Pseudoinverse
blocks.text: Let NinN. We choose quadrature nodes bxi^minS^2 and respective weights w_m>0, m in [M] coloneqq (1, dots, M) such that all spherical harmonics of degree le 2N are exactly integrated by the corresponding quadrature rule, see [GrPo10, HiQu15]. To be more precise, we use the equispaced nodes varphi_i = i pi/(N+1), iin[2N+2], and the Gauss Legendre nodes t_j in [-1,1], jin[N+1], given by the roots of the (N+1) st Legendre polynomial. We denote the corresponding Gauss Legendre weights by r_j. Now we obtain the quadrature bxi^(m(i, j)) coloneqq sph(varphi_i, arccos t_j) quadtext(and)quad w_(m(i, j)) coloneqq 2pi r_j / (2N+2), qquad iin[2N+2], jin[N+1], where m(i, j)in [M] denotes the index related to the pair (i, j) and M=2(N+1)^2. Setting zb f coloneqq (f_m)_(m=1)^M coloneqq (f(bxi^m))_(m=1)^M, quad zb Y_n^k coloneqq (Y_n^k(bxi^m))_(m=1)^M, quadtext(and)quad zb w coloneqq (w_m)_(m=1)^M, we approximate the spherical harmonics coefficients f, Y_n^k by zb f, zb Y_n^k _(bw) coloneqq sum_(m=1)^(M) f(bxi^m) Y_n^k(bxi^m) w_m, qquad n=0, dots, N, k=-n, dots, n. In particular, we have that f, Y_n^k = zb f, zb Y_n^k _(bw) if f is a spherical polynomial of degree le N. All discrete Fourier coefficients can be computed efficiently in bigo(N^2 log^2 N) arithmetic operations utilizing the nonuniform fast spherical Fourier transform (NFSFT) [kupo02, PlPoStTa18]

blocks.heading: Discrete Vertical Slice Transform
blocks.text: For discretizing TtimesII, we use again equispaced nodes psi_i = i pi / (N+1), iin[2N+2] and Gauss Legendre nodes t_j and weights r_j, jin[N+1]. We denote the respective quadrature weights on TtimesII by zb w, where tilde w_(ell(i, j)) = pi r_j / (N+1) and ell(i, j) in [L] with L=2(N+1)^2 denotes the index related to the pair (i, j). The quadrature is exact of degree 2N, i. e., for all linear combinations of basis functions B_n^k with 0le n, k le 2N. Using the singular value decomposition, we discretize V by V_Dcolon R^(M) to R^(L), quad V_Dzb f coloneqq sum_(n=0)^(N) sum_(substack(k=-n +k text(even)) )^n mathrm(v)_n^k inn(zb f, zb Y_n^k)_(bw) zb B_n^k, where zb B_n^k coloneqq (B_n^k(psi_i, t_j))_(ell(i, j)=1)^L and B_n^k is given in. Then V_Dzb f can be computed using the fast Fourier transform (FFT) in psi and a fast polynomial transform [postta98] in t in bigo(N^2 log^3 N) arithmetic operations. Based on the quadrature for T times II, we analogously discretize the (truncated) Moore Penrose pseudoinverse by V^dagger_D colon R^L to R^M, quad V^dagger_D zb g coloneqq sum_(n =0) ^N sum_(substack(k=-n +k text(even)) )^n frac(1)((mathrm v)_n^k) Bigllanglezb g, zb B_n^k Bigrrangle_(tilde (zb w)) zb Y^k_n, where zb g coloneqq (g(psi_i, t_j))_(ell(i, j)=1)^(L) consists of samples of gcolon TtimesII toR. For a spherical polynomial f of degree N, the chosen quadratures ensure V^dagger_DV_D zb f = zb f

blocks.heading: Discrete Semicircle Transform
blocks.text: We use quadrature nodes bQ_ellinSO and weights zb w = (tilde w_(ell))_(ell=1)^L such that all rotational harmonics of degree le 2N are exactly integrated. Since it becomes clear from the context which weights are addressed, we use again zb w. In particular, we consider a quadrature [GrPo09] on SO cong S^2timesS^1 as product of a Gauss-type quadrature on S^2, see [GrPo10], and an equispaced quadrature on T. We use this product structure because we can now discretize W_(alpha, beta) on a uniform grid. Similarly to, the singular value decomposition of Wcolon L^2(S^2) to L^2(SO) can be truncated as mathcal W_Dcolon R^M to R^L, quad mathcal W_Dzb f &coloneqq sum_(n=0)^N sum_(j, k=-n)^(n) lambda_n^j inn(zb f, zb Y_n^k)_(bw) overline(zb D_n^(k, j)), where zb D_n^(k, j) coloneqq (D_n^(k, j)(bQ_ell))_(ell=1)^L. Then can be computed in bigo(N^3 log^2 N + L) arithmetic operations with the nonuniform fast SO(3) Fourier transform (NFSOFT) [poprvo07]. Further, we approximate the Moore Penrose pseudoinverse of W by mathcal W_D^dagger colon R^LtoR^M, quad mathcal W_D^dagger zb g coloneqq sum_(n=0)^N sum_(j, k=-n)^(n) frac(1)((mathrm(w)_n)^2) lambda_n^j inn(zb g, overline(zb D_n^(k, j)))_(tilde(zb w)) zb Y_n^k, where zb g coloneqq (g(bQ_ell))_(ell=1)^L for gcolon SOtoR. As above, W_D^dag zb g can be evaluated with NFSFT and NFSOFT algorithms. For a spherical polynomial f of degree N, we have W^dagger_D W_D zb f = zb f

blocks.heading: Inversion by Variational Approach
blocks.text: The push-forward definitions of the sliced spherical transforms ensure that probability measures are mapped to probability measures. In the context of optimal transport, we require that the inverse transforms have the same behaviour. Even when restricting to the function setting, we can however construct functions with non-trivial negative part that are transformed into probability densities, e. g. by taking a function that is negative in a sufficiently small spherical cap (bxiinS^2: xi_3<1-varepsilon) and equals a positive constant otherwise. Thus the Moore Penrose pseudoinverse applied to a probability density is not necessarily a probability density. To overcome this issue, we consider the inversion of the discretized spherical transforms as inverse problems, which we solve using a variational formulation

blocks.heading: Inversion by Variational Approach
blocks.text: As in, let zb f in R^M contain the samples of the probability density function f on S^2, and zb w in R^M the respective quadrature weights. If the quadrature is exact for f, we have zb fge 0 and int_(S^2) f d sigma_(S^2) = sum_(m=1)^M w_m f_m = 1. Thus zb f can be interpreted as probability density function with respect to the counting measure weighted by bw. For the numerical inversion, we handle both transforms simultaneously, denoting the discretizations V_D and W_D by T_D colon R^M to R^L. Let zb g in R^(L) be the samples of the density function g on T times II or SO. We equip R^M with the weighted Euclidean inner product langle zb f, zb f rangle_(zb w) coloneqq sum_(m=1)^M w_m f_m tilde f_m, and, analogously, R^L with the inner product langle zb g, zb g rangle_( zb w ) coloneqq sum_(ell=1)^L tilde w_ell g_ell tilde g_ell, where zb w contains the quadrature weights for T times II or SO. Furthermore, we denote the all-one vector by zb 1

blocks.heading: Numerical Results
blocks.text: In this section, we provide proof-of-concept examples that the sliced spherical transforms can be combined in a meaningful way with optimal transport on the interval and the circle. First, we deal with the approximation of Wasserstein barycenters on the sphere. In particular, this requires the inversion of the sliced spherical transforms. Second, we show that these transforms combined with optimal transport can be used for classifying classes of measures. All numerical tests are performed in Matlab R2022a on an Intel Core i7-10700 CPU with 16 GB memory

blocks.heading: Interpolation between Probability Measures
blocks.text: Given two probability measures on the sphere, we generate a measure between them, as proposed in [KolParRoh16] for the Radon transform on R^2. In particular, we compute the CDT or cCDT of their spherical transform V or W, then we interpolate in the CDT space and go back to S^2 via the inverse of the CDT or cCDT and the spherical transforms

blocks.heading: Interpolation between Probability Measures
blocks.text: For computing the forward, inverse, and adjoint spherical transforms, we truncate the singular value decomposition at degree N=44 and use the software package [nfft3] for the NFSFT and NFSOFT. We have M = (2N+2)(N+1) = 4050 quadrature nodes on the sphere, cf. sec: disc-and-inv

blocks.heading: Interpolation between Mises Fisher Distributions
blocks.text: As test function on C(S^2), we choose the density of the von Mises Fisher (vMF) distribution f_(kappa, zbeta)(bxi) = c_kappa e^(kappa inn(zbeta, bxi)), quad bxiinS^2, with the mean direction zbetainS^2 and the concentration kappa>0, where c_kappa is chosen such that int_(S^2) f_(kappa, zbeta) dsigma_(S^2) = 1. Since V acts only on even functions, we make our first tests with symmetrized vMF distributions via (f_(kappa, zbeta)(xi_1, xi_2, xi_3) + f_(kappa, zbeta)(xi_1, xi_2, -xi_3))/2, see fig: vmf

blocks.heading: Interpolation between Mises Fisher Distributions
blocks.text: Let mu, nu in Pac(S^2) be two given measures. For some delta in[0,1], we set the unregularized V -CDT interpolation between mu and nu as V^dagger h, quad text(where) quad h(psi, t) = CDT^(-1)_(V_psi mu)big[delta CDT_(V_psi mu)[ V_psi nu]big](t), quad psiinT, tinII. Here, we discretize V_psi via with 2(N+1)^2=4050 quadrature nodes on TtimesII. Our implementation of the CDT and its inverse is based on [KolParRoh16]. Analogously, we define the unregularized W -CDT interpolation W^dagger h, where h(eul(alpha, beta, gamma)) = CDT^(-1)_(W_(alpha, beta) mu)big[ delta sCDT_(W_(alpha, beta) mu)[W_(alpha,beta)nu]big](gamma), quad eul(alpha, beta, gamma)inSO. Here, the optimal parameter theta of, which is required for the sCDT, is determined by the algorithm [DelSalSob10]. Moreover, we compute Wmu and Wnu by, where we use L=118 944 quadrature points eul(alpha, beta, gamma) on SO, which are obtained as the product of a Gauss-type quadrature in sph(alpha, beta) in S^2 and a uniform grid in gamma

blocks.heading: Interpolation between Mises Fisher Distributions
blocks.text: Instead of the Moore Penrose pseudoinverse V^dagger or W^dagger, we also apply the primal-dual alg: class-PD to obtain the regularized inverse of h, which we call the regularized V -CDT or W -CDT interpolation. Here we choose the regularization parameter rho=0. 1 and step sizes sigma=1 and tau=1/4, and we terminate the algorithm after 200 iterations. The CDT interpolations for delta=0. 5 are plotted in fig: vmf_bary. While the regularization has a comparably small effect on the V -CDT interpolation, we note that the unregularized W -CDT interpolation is severely negative in some areas and therefore not a probability density, which is circumvented by the primal-dual algorithm

blocks.heading: Interpolation between Mises Fisher Distributions
blocks.text: As a reference, we consider the spherical 2-Wasserstein barycenter and its entropy-regularized counterpart [PeyCut19], whose computation with the Sinkhorn algorithm [Kni08] can be implemented efficiently, cf. [BaQue22, BenCarCutNenPey15]. We apply the Python optimal transport library [POT] for both, where the Sinkhorn algorithm uses the regularization parameter 0. 01 and a maximum number of 1000 iterations. In our example in fig: vmf_bary, the regularized 2-Wasserstein barycenter looks similar to the W -CDT interpolation, while the unregularized barycenter is very noisy and takes very long to compute with a linear program solver

blocks.heading: Interpolation between vMF Distribution and a Mixture
blocks.text: The W -CDT interpolation of more evolved test functions, which are not symmetric, is depicted in fig: smiley. We notice that the W -CDT interpolation shows the eyes more clearly than the regularized 2-Wasserstein barycenter. This might be caused by a too large regularization parameter of the Sinkhorn algorithm, but when making it smaller the algorithm fails with a division by zero error

blocks.heading: Classification of Probability Measures
blocks.text: In one dimension, the cumulative distribution transform is known to increase the separability between certain classes of probability measures. If the considered classes are build from prototypes using certain transformations like shifts or scalings, the constructed classes are linearly separable in the CDT space [MoCl23, PaKoSo18]. For probability measures on multi-dimensional domains, the separability of the CDT can be exploited by transforming the considered measures to a series of line measures using the Radon or generalized Radon transform [KolParRoh16, KolNadSimBadRoh19]. If we replace the Radon transform by the vertical slice or the normalized semicircle transform, the procedure can be immediately transferred to measures on the sphere

blocks.heading: Classification of Probability Measures
blocks.text: To show that the vertical slice and semicircle transform can in principle improve the separability between different classes of probability measures, we built five datasets consisting of 100 measures each. Each datum represents a (discretized) single or mixture density function of vMF distributions. The concentration is always chosen as kappa = 50. The means are randomly generated on S^2 satisfying the restrictions in tab: dataset. All distributions in the mixtures are equally weighted. fig: vMF-mix shows some examples of the different classes. On the basis of these classes, we train and test linear support vector machines (SVMs) to study the linear separability after our spherical transformations. To be more precise, let f_nu be the density function of a specific datum. This specimen is now transformed into bigl( CDT_(u_II)[V_psi f_nu] bigr)_(psi in T) quadtext(and)quad bigl( sCDT_(u_T)[ W_(alpha,beta) f_nu] bigr)_(sph(alpha, beta) in S^2), where u_bullet denotes the uniform measure. For the numerical implementation, we use the quadrature points bxi^m with N=44 from sec: int-meas

blocks.heading: Classification of Probability Measures
blocks.text: Training and testing of the SVMs is here based on 10-fold cross-validations, i. e., the dataset is divided in 10 subsets containing equally many samples of each class, the training is performed on 9 subsets, and the testing on the remaining. The procedure is repeated 10 times such that each subset serves one time as testing set. Before training, the dimension of the training set is reduced to 50 using a principle component analysis. The success rates of the trained SVMs are given in tab: succ-rate. Although the vertical slice transform cannot distinguish between the upper and lower hemisphere, the V -CDT approach yields high-quality linear separators between the classes of single and mixture vMF densities. The V -CDT approach only fails in experiment #3, which is not surprising since the samples from the second class are seen as single vMF densities by V. The W -CDT approach is useless in #1 and #2, but significantly increases the separability between single and symmetrized vMF distributions. These first simulations show that both spherical transforms can increase the linear separability between certain classes
